english: Let $a$ and $b$ be real numbers and let $f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ be defined by

Suppose that $f$ has a jump discontinuity at $x=0$, that is, $\lim_{x\to0^{-}}f(x)$ and $\lim_{x\to0^{+}}f(x)$ both exist as real numbers and are unequal. Then the value of $\lim_{x\to0^{-}}f(x)$ is ______.
hindi: माना कि $a$ तथा $b$ वास्तविक संख्याएँ हैं तथा $f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ इस प्रकार परिभाषित है

माना कि $x=0$ पर $f$ की उच्छेदी (jump) असांतत्यता है, अर्थात $\lim_{x\to0^{-}}f(x)$ तथा $\lim_{x\to0^{+}}f(x)$ दोनों वास्तविक संख्याओं के रूप में विद्यमान हैं तथा असमान हैं। तब $\lim_{x\to0^{-}}f(x)$ का मान ______ है।
solution: Finite one-sided limits need $a-b=0$ (else $|f|\to\infty$) and then $a-1=0$ (else $f\approx\frac{a-1}{|x|}\to\pm\infty$): $a=b=1$
solution_full: Expand the numerator: $ae^{x}-b-x=(a-b)+(a-1)x+\dfrac{a}{2}x^{2}+O(x^{3})$. The denominator is $x|x|$, with $|x|x||=x^{2}$; it equals $x^{2}$ for $x>0$ and $-x^{2}$ for $x<0$.
If $a\neq b$, the numerator tends to $a-b\neq0$ while the denominator tends to $0$, so $|f(x)|\to\infty$: an infinite discontinuity, not a jump. Hence $a=b$.
If $a=b$ but $a\neq1$, then $f(x)=\dfrac{(a-1)x+O(x^{2})}{x|x|}=\dfrac{a-1}{|x|}+O(1)$, which is unbounded near $0$. Hence $a=1$, and so $b=1$.
The one-sided limits are $-\frac12$ and $\frac12$, both finite and unequal, so this is indeed a jump discontinuity.
originality_note: New: the type of the discontinuity (jump, not infinite) is used as the condition that determines the parameters, and the sign of x|x| then splits the one-sided limits (way 5). Closest known: choose constants so that (e^x - 1 - ax)/x^2 has a finite limit. Different because: the denominator x|x| makes the finite limits opposite, so the answer depends on the side and the classification of the discontinuity is the given condition.
key_step: Finite one-sided limits force a = b = 1; then the sign of x|x| on the left gives -1/2.
justification: Routine chain: two orders of the expansion fix a and b, then a one-sided limit with |x|. Same demand as 2025-P2-Q1 (L2) on limits with an absolute value.

concept_use.Types of discontinuity: A jump discontinuity needs both one-sided limits finite (excluding the infinite type), which forces a = b = 1; the limits -1/2 and 1/2 confirm it is a jump.

stem_review: Read as a student: a, b and f (domain, codomain, value at 0) are defined; 'jump discontinuity' is explained in the stem so there is one reading. Checked with sympy that the left limit is -1/2 and the right limit 1/2. Answer -0.50, a negative decimal. Changed: added the explanation of jump discontinuity in the stem.
